item.title: Energy Production: How Your Body Creates ATP
item.description:
How Energy Production Works

Your body converts food into usable energy through a sophisticated system of biochemical reactions. The fundamental unit of energy in your body is ATP (adenosine triphosphate), a small molecule that stores energy in its chemical bonds.

The Three Stages of Energy Production

1. Glycolysis (Cytoplasm)

  • Glucose (or amino acids/fatty acids) enters the cytoplasm
  • Broken down into 2 pyruvate molecules
  • Produces a net of 2 ATP molecules and 2 NADH
  • Does NOT require oxygen (anaerobic)
  • Fast energy source, useful for explosive activities

2. Citric Acid Cycle (Mitochondrial Matrix)

item.title: Copper
item.description:
What Is Copper?

Copper is an essential trace mineral involved in critical processes including iron metabolism, collagen crosslinking, energy production, and immune function. Despite being essential, copper toxicity is a more common concern than deficiency in modern populations.

Copper exists in two oxidation states: Cu+ (cuprous) and Cu2+ (cupric). The human body carefully regulates copper through chelation proteins, particularly ceruloplasmin, which binds ~95% of serum copper and prevents oxidative damage.

item.title: Vitamin B1 (Thiamine)
item.description:
What Is Vitamin B1?

Vitamin B1 (thiamine) is a water-soluble B vitamin that serves as a critical coenzyme in carbohydrate metabolism, energy production, and nervous system function. Unlike most vitamins, thiamine cannot be synthesized by the human body and has no significant storage capacity — daily intake is essential.

Biochemistry: Thiamine is converted to thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), the active coenzyme form. TPP is required by three key enzymes: pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase. These enzymes occupy central positions in glucose metabolism and the pentose phosphate pathway (critical for NADPH production and biosynthesis).

item.title: Vitamin B2 (Riboflavin)
item.description:
What Is Vitamin B2?

Vitamin B2 (riboflavin) is an essential water-soluble B vitamin that serves as the precursor to two critical coenzymes: flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) and flavin mononucleotide (FMN). These flavins are absolutely central to energy production, as they accept and donate electrons throughout the electron transport chain and in numerous metabolic pathways.

item.title: Vitamin B3 (Niacin)
item.description:
What Is Vitamin B3 (Niacin)?

Vitamin B3, also known as niacin, nicotinic acid, or vitamin PP (pellagra-preventing), exists as multiple chemical entities with different biochemical functions and biohacking implications. Understanding these distinctions is critical for optimizing outcomes:

Nicotinic Acid (Niacin): The original form recognized to prevent pellagra (severe deficiency disease); provides the flush response and most potent therapeutic effects on lipid profiles and NAD+ elevation.

Nicotinamide (Niacinamide): The non-flushing form; functions as a direct NAD+ precursor but lacks the lipid-modifying and flushing effects of nicotinic acid—important distinction for protocol selection.

item.title: Vitamin B5 (Pantothenic Acid)
item.description:
What Is Vitamin B5?

Vitamin B5 (pantothenic acid) is a water-soluble B vitamin with a unique metabolic role: it is the precursor to Coenzyme A (CoA), one of the most critical molecules in human metabolism. CoA is involved in literally thousands of enzymatic reactions — any reaction involving acetyl groups or acyl groups requires CoA.

Biochemistry: Pantothenic acid is converted through a multi-step process:

  1. Pantothenic acid → Pantothenate
  2. Pantothenate + Cysteine → Pantetheine (via pantotheinase)
  3. Pantetheine → CoA (via PPCDC enzyme)
